Australia Income Tax Brackets 2026-27: What Your Salary Actually Costs in Tax

Published: 2 May 2026 · Last updated: June 2026 · By James O'Brien, CPA

If you have ever stared at your payslip and wondered where a big chunk of your salary went, this guide will answer that clearly and honestly. From 1 July 2026, Australia's income tax brackets have changed — and if any article or calculator is still showing 19% or 32.5% for the lower brackets, those numbers are wrong. The Stage 3 tax cuts legislated in 2024 have continued to roll forward, and FY2026-27 brings one further rate reduction that every working Australian should understand.

This article covers the correct 2026-27 tax brackets, how the progressive system actually works, detailed take-home pay calculations at common salary levels, and what tools you can use to model your own situation.

What Changed From 1 July 2026

Australia's tax system went through a significant structural shift with the Stage 3 tax cuts that took effect from 1 July 2024. Those changes lowered the second-bracket rate from 19% to 16% and collapsed the former 32.5% and 37% brackets into a single 30% band stretching from $45,001 to $135,000. FY2025-26 saw that second bracket sit at 16%.

From 1 July 2026 — the start of FY2026-27 — one further legislated change comes into effect: the rate on income between $18,201 and $45,000 drops again, from 16% to 15%. Every other bracket remains unchanged. The saving is modest — up to $268 per year for most earners — but it is automatic and applies through your employer's payroll without any action on your part.

The Correct FY2026-27 Income Tax Brackets

The following table shows the official ATO resident income tax rates for FY2026-27. These do not include the Medicare levy, which is covered separately below.

Taxable Income Range Marginal Tax Rate Maximum Tax in This Band
$0 – $18,2000%$0
$18,201 – $45,00015%$4,020
$45,001 – $135,00030%$27,000
$135,001 – $190,00037%$20,350
$190,001 and above45%Uncapped

Adding the Medicare levy of 2% brings the effective marginal rates to 0%, 17%, 32%, 39%, and 47% at each level. These are the rates that govern decisions about salary sacrifice, investment income, and deductions.

Important: If you have seen articles, calculators, or tables showing 19% for the second bracket or 32.5% for the middle bracket — those figures reflect pre-2024 rates. They are outdated for any financial year from 2024-25 onwards, and entirely incorrect for 2026-27.

How the Progressive System Works

Australia taxes income in layers, not as a flat percentage of everything you earn. Think of it as filling buckets: the first $18,200 fills at 0%, the next portion fills at 15%, and so on. Only the dollars that fall within each bracket are taxed at that bracket's rate.

This means your marginal rate — the rate applied to the next dollar you earn — is always higher than your effective rate, which is your total tax bill expressed as a percentage of your total income. The marginal rate tells you what a pay rise, a deduction, or a salary sacrifice is actually worth. The effective rate tells you what fraction of your income is actually paid to the ATO.

What You Actually Take Home: Worked Examples at Key Salary Levels

The following calculations are based on a standard Australian resident with no HECS-HELP debt, no salary sacrifice, and no deductions beyond the standard tax-free threshold. The Low Income Tax Offset (LITO) is applied where eligible.

On a $60,000 Salary

  • $0 to $18,200 — $0 tax
  • $18,201 to $45,000 — $26,800 × 15% = $4,020
  • $45,001 to $60,000 — $15,000 × 30% = $4,500
  • Gross income tax: $8,520
  • LITO: $700 − ($15,000 × 1.5%) = $700 − $225 = $475 offset
  • Net income tax: $8,520 − $475 = $8,045
  • Medicare levy (2%): $60,000 × 2% = $1,200
  • Total tax and Medicare: approximately $9,245
  • Take-home pay: approximately $50,755/year ($976/week)
  • Effective tax rate: ~15.4%

On a $90,000 Salary

At $90,000, LITO is fully phased out (it ceases above $66,667). The entire income above $45,000 sits in the 30% bracket.

  • $0 to $18,200 — $0
  • $18,201 to $45,000 — $26,800 × 15% = $4,020
  • $45,001 to $90,000 — $45,000 × 30% = $13,500
  • Gross income tax: $17,520
  • LITO: $0 (fully phased out)
  • Medicare levy: $90,000 × 2% = $1,800
  • Total tax and Medicare: approximately $19,320
  • Take-home pay: approximately $70,680/year ($1,359/week)
  • Effective tax rate: ~21.5%

On a $120,000 Salary

  • $0 to $18,200 — $0
  • $18,201 to $45,000 — $26,800 × 15% = $4,020
  • $45,001 to $120,000 — $75,000 × 30% = $22,500
  • Gross income tax: $26,520
  • LITO: $0
  • Medicare levy: $120,000 × 2% = $2,400
  • Total tax and Medicare: approximately $28,920
  • Take-home pay: approximately $91,080/year ($1,751/week)
  • Effective tax rate: ~24.1%

On a $180,000 Salary

At this level the earner spans three brackets and enters the 37% band above $135,000:

  • $0 to $18,200 — $0
  • $18,201 to $45,000 — $26,800 × 15% = $4,020
  • $45,001 to $135,000 — $90,000 × 30% = $27,000
  • $135,001 to $180,000 — $45,000 × 37% = $16,650
  • Gross income tax: $47,670
  • LITO: $0
  • Medicare levy: $180,000 × 2% = $3,600
  • Total tax and Medicare: approximately $51,270
  • Take-home pay: approximately $128,730/year ($2,475/week)
  • Effective tax rate: ~28.5%

The Low Income Tax Offset (LITO) in 2026-27

The LITO is a direct reduction of the tax you owe — applied after the bracket calculation is done. It is not a deduction from income. For 2026-27:

  • Maximum LITO: $700 (for taxable income up to $37,500)
  • Phases out at 5 cents per dollar between $37,500 and $45,000
  • Further reduced at 1.5 cents per dollar between $45,001 and $66,667
  • Nil above $66,667

The practical effect of LITO is to push the real tax-free threshold well above $18,200. A person earning around $22,575 would owe a small amount of tax on income above $18,200 — but the LITO credit eliminates it entirely, making the effective tax-free amount approximately $22,575 for eligible lower-income earners in 2026-27.

The Medicare Levy and the Surcharge

The Medicare levy of 2% applies on top of income tax for most Australian residents. Low-income earners are exempt below approximately $26,000, with a gradual phase-in zone above that.

Higher earners should also be aware of the Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS). If your income exceeds approximately $93,000 (for singles in 2026-27) and you do not hold an appropriate private hospital cover policy, you pay an additional surcharge on top of the standard 2% levy. Surcharge rates: 1% (up to $108,000), 1.25% (up to $144,000), 1.5% (above $144,001). For many earners in the $100,000–$130,000 range, taking out private hospital cover can save money versus paying the MLS.

How HECS-HELP Debt Affects Your Take-Home Pay

If you have a HECS-HELP student loan, your employer withholds an additional repayment percentage from your pay based on gross income — separate from income tax but deducted through the same PAYG withholding system. The repayment threshold for 2026-27 sits at approximately $54,435. Above that, repayment rates range from around 1% to 10% of total income. On a $90,000 salary, the mandatory HECS repayment rate is approximately 3.5%, adding around $3,150 per year — meaning real take-home falls to around $67,530, not $70,680.

Salary Sacrifice: Using the Brackets to Your Advantage

Salary sacrifice into superannuation reduces your assessable income before tax is applied. Contributions go into your super fund and are taxed at a flat 15% — significantly lower than the marginal rates most working Australians face. Consider someone earning $150,000: their income above $135,000 is taxed at 37% plus Medicare. If this person salary sacrifices $20,000 into super, their taxable income drops to $130,000 — keeping them entirely within the 30% bracket. The $20,000 is taxed at 15% inside super instead of a blended rate approaching 39%.

The concessional (pre-tax) super contribution cap for 2026-27 is $30,000, which includes your employer's compulsory 11.5% Superannuation Guarantee contributions.

PAYG Withholding: How the ATO Collects Tax During the Year

Your employer deducts the estimated tax from each pay under the Pay As You Go (PAYG) withholding system, using ATO tax tables updated to reflect the 15% rate from 1 July 2026 — your withholding amounts will automatically reduce slightly in the new financial year. At the end of the year, when you lodge your tax return (due by 31 October for self-lodgers), the ATO reconciles actual tax owed against what was withheld. Since Single Touch Payroll (STP) became universal, your employer reports each pay event in real time and the ATO's pre-filled myTax already contains your salary and withholding data.

FY2026-27 vs Previous Years: A Quick Comparison

The table below shows how the second bracket has evolved since the Stage 3 cuts took effect.

Financial Year $18,201–$45,000 Rate $45,001–$135,000 Rate
2023-24 (pre-Stage 3)19%32.5%
2024-2516%30%
2025-2616%30%
2026-2715%30%

If any financial tool — calculator, article, or payroll system — still shows 19% and 32.5% for the second and third brackets in 2026-27, those figures are incorrect and should be updated immediately.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • What are the income tax brackets in Australia for FY2026-27?

    For Australian residents in 2026-27, the brackets are: 0% on income up to $18,200; 15% on $18,201 to $45,000; 30% on $45,001 to $135,000; 37% on $135,001 to $190,000; and 45% on income above $190,000. The Medicare levy of 2% applies on top for most taxpayers. Figures of 19% or 32.5% reflect outdated pre-2024 brackets.

  • How much tax do I pay on a $90,000 salary in Australia in 2026-27?

    On a $90,000 salary with no deductions or offsets beyond the standard rates, you pay approximately $17,520 in income tax plus $1,800 in Medicare levy — a total of around $19,320. Your effective tax rate is approximately 21.5%, even though your marginal rate (including Medicare) is 32%.

  • What is the tax-free threshold in Australia in 2026-27?

    The official tax-free threshold is $18,200. With the Low Income Tax Offset (LITO) applied, the practical tax-free amount rises to approximately $22,575, meaning lower-income earners at or below this level pay no income tax at all.

  • What changed in the 2026-27 tax year specifically?

    The only bracket change from 1 July 2026 is a reduction in the second bracket rate from 16% to 15% on income between $18,201 and $45,000. All other brackets remain identical to 2025-26. The saving is worth up to $268 per year and is applied automatically through PAYG withholding — no action is needed by the employee.

  • Does the Medicare levy change in 2026-27?

    The Medicare levy remains at 2% of taxable income for most residents in 2026-27. The Medicare Levy Surcharge (an additional 1% to 1.5%) continues to apply to higher-income earners without private hospital cover. The low-income levy exemption threshold is updated annually by the ATO.

  • How do I reduce my income tax legally in Australia?

    The most effective strategies include salary sacrificing into superannuation (contributions taxed at 15% inside the fund rather than your marginal rate), claiming legitimate work-related deductions, making personal deductible super contributions, and — for those above the $93,000 MLS threshold — taking out private hospital cover. Each strategy has different eligibility rules depending on your income level. Consult a registered tax agent to model the options for your specific situation.
